topic: The Earliest Sunset Isn't on the Shortest Day
angle: In much of the Northern Hemisphere, the earliest sunset comes about two weeks before the winter solstice.
brief: Show a calendar with sunset times ticking earlier, then starting to move later in early December, while the days are still getting shorter. Explain the equation of time: Earth's tilt and its oval orbit make solar noon drift against clock time around the solstice. Show the sunrise and sunset markers both sliding later together. End with the takeaway: the solstice is still the shortest day, but it doesn't have the earliest sunset.
reason: It's a surprising fact about something people notice every day as the evenings get darker.

evidence.title: Why Isn't the Year's Earliest Sunset on the Winter Solstice? (timeanddate)
Equation of time (timeanddate)

topic: Why Cold Weather Makes You Need to Pee
angle: It isn't just in your head: being cold makes your body produce more urine, and it has a name, cold diuresis.
brief: Show a character stepping into the cold and immediately hunting for a bathroom. Animate blood vessels in the skin narrowing to keep heat in, which pushes more blood toward the body's core and raises blood pressure. Show the kidneys reacting by removing extra fluid. Note that scientists still debate the details, and finish with a reminder to stay hydrated in winter.
reason: Lots of people notice this in winter but don't know the reason.

evidence.title: Why does cold weather make me need to pee? (AccuWeather)
Why Do We Urinate More When It's Cold? (ScienceABC)

topic: Do You Really Lose Most Heat Through Your Head?
angle: Your head isn't a heat chimney. It loses about as much heat as any other uncovered skin.
brief: Show a thermal camera view of a person in a coat but no hat, with the head glowing, then reveal that the rest of their body is covered. Explain that the myth is often traced to old military cold-weather tests where the head was the only uncovered part. Show the numbers: the head is about 10% of the body's surface and loses about 7–10% of body heat. End with: still wear a hat, but cover everything else too.
reason: It's winter advice everyone has heard, and the explanation is simple.

evidence.title: Monday's medical myth: you lose most heat through your head (The Conversation)
The great cold head myth (BBC Science Focus)

angle: The idea that poinsettias are deadly comes largely from a 1919 rumor that was never proven.
brief: Show a holiday plant with a skull-and-crossbones tag, then peel the tag off. Tell the story of the 1919 rumor about a child's death, which was later repeated as fact in print even though no link was found. Show the evidence: poison-control data covering more than 20,000 cases with no deaths. Add the honest caveat that the milky sap can irritate skin and upset stomachs, so keep it away from pets and kids anyway.
reason: It fits the holiday season, and the story behind the rumor is surprising.

evidence.title: Poinsettia's Poisonous Reputation Persists, Despite Proof to the Contrary (Ohio State CFAES)

topic: Fall Colors Were Hiding All Summer
angle: The yellow and orange in autumn leaves were there all year. The green was just covering them up.
brief: Show a green leaf as layered paint, with chlorophyll on top and yellow-orange carotenoids underneath. As the days get shorter, the chlorophyll breaks down and the hidden colors appear. Explain that reds are different: many trees make new red pigments (anthocyanins) in autumn, especially after sunny days and cool nights. End with why oaks often turn brown.
reason: A familiar seasonal sight gets an unexpected explanation that's easy to animate.

evidence.title: Why Leaves Change Color in Fall (UC Davis Arboretum)

angle: Scientists did find two matching snowflakes, but only the very simple kind.
brief: Follow a tiny ice crystal falling through a cloud, picking up new branches as the temperature and humidity change, so each path makes a different flake. Explain why big, fully formed flakes are almost certainly unique. Then the twist: in 1988 researcher Nancy Knight found two identical hollow-column crystals, and simple crystals can also be grown almost identically in a lab. End by asking which version of 'unique' counts.
reason: It's a familiar saying with a twist that's mostly true, just as winter arrives.

topic: The Frog That Freezes Solid and Comes Back to Life
angle: This frog's heart stops all winter, and in spring it starts beating again.
brief: Open on a wood frog frozen hard as an ice cube under the leaf litter, with no heartbeat and no breathing. An animated cutaway shows ice forming outside its cells while the liver floods the body with glucose that acts as a natural antifreeze. Then fast-forward to spring: the frog thaws, its heart restarts and it hops away. End with the line: 'Scientists still aren't sure what restarts the heart.'
reason: The 'dead in winter, alive in spring' reveal is strange enough to keep people watching, and it fits the start of winter.

topic: Can You Really See the Great Wall from Space?
angle: The 'only human-made thing visible from space' is almost invisible from orbit.
brief: Start with the famous claim on screen, then zoom out from the Great Wall to the Space Station's view. Show why it's hard to spot: the wall is only about as wide as a road and is roughly the same color as the land around it. Add that astronauts, including China's first astronaut, reported they couldn't see it with the naked eye. End with the twist that the claim appeared in a 1932 Ripley's cartoon, decades before anyone went to space.
reason: Almost everyone has heard this 'fact', and proving it wrong with a clear visual is very satisfying.

topic: The Doctor Who Cracked One Hand for 60 Years
angle: One doctor tested the knuckle-cracking myth on himself for about 60 years.
brief: Show a split screen of two hands: the left one cracks its knuckles twice a day for decades and the right one never does. Explain the pop as a gas bubble forming in the joint fluid, not bones grinding. Reveal the result: neither hand got arthritis, and the experiment won an Ig Nobel Prize. Close by noting that larger studies agree there's no link to arthritis, but that it was still only a test on one person.
reason: It's a habit millions of people have, and a quirky experiment makes a memorable payoff.

topic: Do We Only Use 10% of Our Brains?
angle: If 90% of your brain were unused, damage to most of it wouldn't matter, and it does.
brief: Start with a brain that's 90% greyed out, then light it up region by region with labels such as vision, movement, speech and memory. Explain that damage to almost any area causes some loss of ability, and that the brain is about 2% of body weight but uses about 20% of the body's energy. End with the point that most of the brain is active nearly all the time, even during sleep.
reason: It's one of the most widely believed science myths and is easy to show visually.

topic: Lightning Does Strike Twice, About 20+ Times a Year
angle: One New York skyscraper is hit by lightning about 20 to 25 times a year.
brief: Open on the old saying 'lightning never strikes the same place twice', then show a storm with bolt after bolt hitting the Empire State Building. Explain that lightning favors tall, pointed, conductive objects, so the same spot can be hit again and again. Show the lightning rod and grounding system guiding the current safely into the ground. End with a safety line: if you've been struck nearby, the danger hasn't passed.
reason: The bolts give it an instant hook, and it overturns a saying everyone knows.

topic: This Week's Shooting Stars Are Comet Dust
angle: Tonight's shooting stars are specks of comet dust no bigger than a grain of sand.
brief: Tie the video to the Leonid meteor shower, which peaks on the night of November 17–18. Animate Earth crossing the trail of debris left by Comet Tempel-Tuttle, with tiny grains burning up at about 70 km per second. Add the historical twist that in 1833 the Leonids produced a storm of thousands of meteors per hour. End with viewing tips: after midnight, dark skies, look toward the constellation Leo.
reason: It's timely, a real sky event happens that week, and there's a clear 'go outside and look' call to action.

topic: Why Winter Turns You Into a Static Shock Machine
angle: That doorknob zap is a tiny lightning bolt, and dry winter air is to blame.
brief: Show a slow-motion zap between a fingertip and a doorknob. Explain that walking and rubbing fabrics build up electric charge on your body. In humid air a thin film of moisture lets that charge leak away, but cold air holds little water and indoor heating dries it out even more, so the charge builds until it jumps. End with simple fixes: humidify the air, or touch metal with a key first.
reason: It's an everyday annoyance that starts right now, and the zap makes a great visual hook.

evidence.title: Why do static shocks happen in winter? (University of Kentucky Physics)

topic: Why Geese Fly in a V
angle: Birds in a V formation ride the swirling air off the wingtips of the bird in front.
brief: Use an overhead view of a migrating V and add visible swirling air currents coming off each wingtip. Show how each trailing bird sits in rising air and times its wingbeats to the bird ahead, which saves energy on long trips. Include the GPS-tracking study of northern bald ibises that showed this in real flight, and that the birds rotate who leads. Keep the size of the savings general, because estimates vary.
reason: Lots of people see migrating flocks in autumn, and the hidden airflow makes a nice reveal.

evidence.title: Why Do Birds Fly in a V Formation? (Audubon)

topic: Can a Fuzzy Caterpillar Predict Winter?
angle: Folklore says this caterpillar's stripes forecast winter, so do they?
brief: Show a woolly bear crawling across the screen with its black and brown bands labeled 'mild' and 'harsh'. Explain where the legend came from: a 1940s entomologist's small, informal count was reported in the newspapers. Reveal the real cause: the bands change with the caterpillar's age, species and how long it has been feeding, and may say more about the previous season than the coming one. End with a tip: the real forecast comes from ocean and atmosphere data.
reason: It's a fall tradition people are seeing right now, and the answer is quick and clear.

topic: Your Breath Is a Tiny Cloud
angle: When you see your breath on a cold day, you're making your own little cloud.
brief: Zoom into a puff of breath on a cold morning and down to the molecules: warm, moist air from the lungs hits cold air, and the water vapor condenses into millions of tiny droplets that scatter light. Explain that humidity matters as well as temperature, so on dry, cold days you may not see your breath at all. End by showing the same process making fog and clouds.
reason: It's an everyday winter moment people are noticing now, with a simple 'aha' explanation.
